content: Drains are frequently used in leg wounds following vascular surgery, although their benefits remain uncertain. The primary purpose of placing drains is to reduce the accumulation of blood or fluid in the surgical site. However, the use of drains may also increase the risk of infection and potentially extend the duration of hospital stays. Surgeons require reliable evidence to determine whether the use of drains reduces complications after lower limb arterial surgery. The objective of this review was to assess whether the routine use of wound drains leads to fewer complications compared to not using drains in lower limb arterial surgery. A comprehensive search was conducted in June 2016 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL. Clinical trial registries were also searched for ongoing studies. No restrictions were applied regarding language, publication date, or study setting. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the use of any type of drain in lower limb arterial surgery. Two independent authors assessed the eligibility of studies, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. Efforts were made to contact study authors for missing data. The findings of eligible studies were summarized, and meta-analyses were planned if clinical and statistical homogeneity allowed. Three trials, involving 222 participants and 333 groin wounds, met the inclusion criteria. All studies compared suction drainage with no drainage. Two trials were parallel-group RCTs, while one was a split-body RCT. The settings of the trials were not clearly described. Participants underwent bypass and endarterectomy procedures, but none of the studies provided information on the severity of the underlying arterial disease. All three studies were judged to have a high risk of bias in at least three domains, and the overall quality of evidence was very low. Two of the three studies had significant unit-of-analysis errors, as they treated multiple wounds within the same patient as independent observations. The appropriateness of the analysis in the third study could not be determined. Due to clinical heterogeneity and the inability to adjust for analysis errors, meta-analysis was not feasible. One trial provided data on surgical site infections (SSI), the primary outcome of interest. This trial found no clear difference in SSI rates between drained and non-drained wounds (risk ratio 1.33; 95% confidence interval 0.30 to 5.94; 50 participants with bilateral groin wounds; very low-quality evidence). Other outcomes from this trial could not be evaluated. The results from the remaining two studies were deemed unreliable due to analysis errors and incomplete reporting. In conclusion, the evidence available to guide clinical practice in this area is limited and subject to significant biases. There remains complete uncertainty regarding the potential benefits and harms of using wound drains in lower limb arterial surgery. The small number of studies, combined with their methodological weaknesses, prevents any definitive conclusions. High-quality research is urgently needed to inform clinical decision-making. To the best of our knowledge, no ongoing trials are currently addressing this topic.
